images/art/couverture.jpg.caption: Rembrandt, Philosopher in Meditation (1632, Paris, Musée du Louvre).
images/art/couverture.jpg.alt: An old man seated by a window, beside a spiral staircase sunk in shadow

images/auteurs/epicure.jpg.caption: Epicurus, marble portrait, Roman copy of a Greek original (Rome, Museo Nazionale Romano, Palazzo Massimo).

images/auteurs/lucrece.png.caption: Lucretius: no authentic portrait is known; this effigy is conventional.

images/auteurs/eckhart.jpg.caption: Figure traditionally identified as Meister Eckhart, detail of the fresco by Andrea di Bonaiuto, Spanish Chapel, Santa Maria Novella, Florence (c. 1365-1367); no authentic portrait exists.

images/auteurs/pascal.jpg.caption: Blaise Pascal, engraving by Gérard Edelinck.

images/auteurs/hume.jpg.caption: David Hume, portrait by Allan Ramsay.

images/auteurs/voltaire.jpg.caption: Voltaire, portrait by Nicolas de Largillière (Paris, Musée Carnavalet).

images/auteurs/holbach.jpg.caption: Paul Henri Thiry d'Holbach, portrait by Alexander Roslin.

images/auteurs/stirner.jpg.caption: Max Stirner, detail of Engels's drawing of the Freien (1842); the only likenesses of him we have are sketches by Engels.

images/auteurs/comte.jpg.caption: Auguste Comte, portrait kept at the Maison d'Auguste Comte, Paris.

images/auteurs/schopenhauer.jpg.caption: Arthur Schopenhauer, photograph by J. Schäfer (1859).

images/auteurs/dostoievski.jpg.caption: Dostoevsky, portrait by Vasily Perov (1872, Moscow, Tretyakov Gallery).

images/auteurs/william-james.jpg.caption: William James, photograph by Alice Boughton (c. 1907): “The Will to Believe” (1896) is a direct reply to Clifford.

images/auteurs/freud.jpg.caption: Sigmund Freud, photograph by Max Halberstadt.

images/auteurs/schmitt.jpg.caption: Carl Schmitt in 1904, detail of a class photograph.

images/auteurs/comte-sponville.jpg.caption: André Comte-Sponville at the Salon du livre de Paris, 2014.

images/auteurs/ferry.jpg.caption: Luc Ferry at the Salon du livre de Paris, 2017.

images/oeuvres/pascal-memorial.jpg.caption: Pascal's Memorial (night of 23 November 1654), facsimile of the autograph in the Brunschvicg edition: the sheet bearing the “Dieu d'Abraham, Dieu d'Isaac, Dieu de Jacob, non des philosophes et des savants” (God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, not of the philosophers and scholars).
images/oeuvres/pascal-memorial.jpg.alt: Manuscript sheet covered in dense handwriting, with a cross at the top

images/art/rembrandt-sacrifice-isaac.jpg.caption: Rembrandt, The Sacrifice of Isaac (1635, Saint Petersburg, Hermitage): the God of Abraham and Isaac, whom the Memorial sets against the God of the philosophers.
images/art/rembrandt-sacrifice-isaac.jpg.alt: An angel holds back Abraham's arm as he is about to cut Isaac's throat; the knife falls

images/art/michel-ange-isaie.jpg.caption: Michelangelo, the prophet Isaiah, Sistine Chapel ceiling (1508-1512): Isaiah is the prophet of the hidden God, Deus absconditus (Is 45, 15), at the heart of the Pensées.
images/art/michel-ange-isaie.jpg.alt: The prophet Isaiah seated, a closed book under his hand, turning towards a child

images/oeuvres/spinoza-tractatus-1670.jp.caption: Title page of the Tractatus theologico-politicus (1670), published without the author's name and under a false printer's address in Hamburg: the book in which Spinoza subjects Scripture to historical criticism.
images/oeuvres/spinoza-tractatus-1670.jp.alt: Title page of the Tractatus theologico-politicus, printed in Latin

images/oeuvres/bayle-pensees-comete.jpg.caption: Title page of the Pensées diverses écrites à un docteur de Sorbonne à l'occasion de la comète (sixth edition, 1749): the book of the hypothesis of a society of atheists, born of the comet of December 1680.
images/oeuvres/bayle-pensees-comete.jpg.alt: Title page of the Pensées diverses sur la comète, 1749 edition

images/oeuvres/hume-dialogues-1779.jpg.caption: Title page of the Dialogues concerning Natural Religion (1779), published three years after the death of Hume, who had kept them unpublished in his lifetime.
images/oeuvres/hume-dialogues-1779.jpg.alt: Title page of the Dialogues concerning Natural Religion, 1779

images/oeuvres/holbach-systeme-nature-17.caption: Title page of the Système de la nature (1770), published under the name of Mirabaud, who had died ten years earlier, and under the fictitious imprint of London.
images/oeuvres/holbach-systeme-nature-17.alt: Title page of the Système de la nature, attributed to M. Mirabaud, London, 1770

images/oeuvres/kant-religion-1793.jpg.caption: Title page of Die Religion innerhalb der Grenzen der bloßen Vernunft (1793), the book that earned Kant the royal reprimand of 1794.
images/oeuvres/kant-religion-1793.jpg.alt: Title page of Die Religion innerhalb der Grenzen der bloßen Vernunft, 1793

images/oeuvres/schleiermacher-uber-die-r.caption: Title page of Über die Religion. Reden an die Gebildeten unter ihren Verächtern (1799), published without the author's name.
images/oeuvres/schleiermacher-uber-die-r.alt: Title page of Über die Religion, 1799

images/oeuvres/strauss-leben-jesu-1835.j.caption: Title page of the first volume of Das Leben Jesu, kritisch bearbeitet (1835), which makes myth the central category of the criticism of the Gospels.
images/oeuvres/strauss-leben-jesu-1835.j.alt: Title page of the first volume of Strauss's Das Leben Jesu

images/oeuvres/renan-vie-de-jesus-1863.j.caption: Title page of the Vie de Jésus (1863), first volume of the Histoire des origines du christianisme.
images/oeuvres/renan-vie-de-jesus-1863.j.alt: Title page of Ernest Renan's Vie de Jésus, 1863

images/oeuvres/feuerbach-wesen-des-chris.caption: Title page of Das Wesen des Christenthums (Leipzig, Otto Wigand, 1841).
images/oeuvres/feuerbach-wesen-des-chris.alt: Title page in Gothic type of Das Wesen des Christenthums, Leipzig, 1841

images/oeuvres/stirner-der-einzige.png.caption: Title page of Der Einzige und sein Eigenthum (Leipzig, Otto Wigand), published in October 1844 with the date 1845.
images/oeuvres/stirner-der-einzige.png.alt: Title page of Der Einzige und sein Eigenthum

images/oeuvres/marx-kapital-1867.png.caption: Title page of the first volume of Das Kapital (Hamburg, Otto Meissner, 1867), in facsimile.
images/oeuvres/marx-kapital-1867.png.alt: Title page of the first volume of Das Kapital, Hamburg, 1867

images/oeuvres/comte-catechisme-positivi.caption: Title page of the Catéchisme positiviste (1852), “sommaire exposition de la religion universelle” (summary exposition of the universal religion) in conversations between a woman and a priest of Humanity.
images/oeuvres/comte-catechisme-positivi.alt: Title page of the Catéchisme positiviste, Paris, 1852

images/oeuvres/schopenhauer-welt-1819.jp.caption: First edition of Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung (Leipzig, Brockhaus, dated 1819, published at the end of 1818).
images/oeuvres/schopenhauer-welt-1819.jp.alt: Open copy of the first edition of Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung

images/oeuvres/dostoievski-karamazov.jpg.caption: The Brothers Karamazov in the Russky Vestnik, where the novel appeared as a serial (1879-1880).
images/oeuvres/dostoievski-karamazov.jpg.alt: Printed page in Russian bearing the title The Brothers Karamazov

images/oeuvres/nietzsche-frohliche-wisse.caption: Title page of the first edition of Die fröhliche Wissenschaft (1882), in which the madman who announces the death of God appears, in § 125.
images/oeuvres/nietzsche-frohliche-wisse.alt: Title page of the first edition of Die fröhliche Wissenschaft, 1882

images/oeuvres/durkheim-formes-elementai.caption: Les Formes élémentaires de la vie religieuse (1912), in which Durkheim makes the sacred the matrix of society.
images/oeuvres/durkheim-formes-elementai.alt: Title page of Les Formes élémentaires de la vie religieuse, 1912

images/oeuvres/james-varieties-1902.jpg.caption: Cover of The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902), drawn from the Gifford Lectures given in Edinburgh in 1901-1902.
images/oeuvres/james-varieties-1902.jpg.alt: Cover of The Varieties of Religious Experience, 1902

images/oeuvres/freud-zukunft-einer-illus.caption: Cover of the first edition of Die Zukunft einer Illusion (1927).
images/oeuvres/freud-zukunft-einer-illus.alt: Cover of the first edition of Die Zukunft einer Illusion, 1927

images/auteurs/george-eliot.jpg.caption: George Eliot, portrait by François D'Albert Durade: the translator of Feuerbach, she published The Essence of Christianity in 1854 under her name Marian Evans.
images/auteurs/george-eliot.jpg.alt: Portrait of George Eliot as a young woman, seated

images/auteurs/romain-rolland.jpg.caption: Romain Rolland in 1915: it is his letter on the “sentiment océanique” (oceanic feeling) that Freud answers at the beginning of Das Unbehagen in der Kultur (1930).

images/art/velazquez-christ-crucifie.jpg.caption: Velázquez, Christ Crucified (c. 1632, Madrid, Prado): the speculative Good Friday, in which Hegel takes up the “Gott selbst ist tot” of the Lutheran hymn.
images/art/velazquez-christ-crucifie.jpg.alt: Christ on the cross against a black background, his head bowed

images/art/duccio-tentation.jpg.caption: Duccio, The Temptation of Christ on the Mountain (1308-1311, New York, Frick Collection), a panel from the Siena Maestà: the temptations that the Grand Inquisitor takes up.
images/art/duccio-tentation.jpg.alt: Christ on a mountain repels the devil; at his feet, miniature cities

images/art/berruguete-autodafe.jpg.caption: Pedro Berruguete, Saint Dominic Presiding over an Auto-da-fé (c. 1493-1499, Madrid, Prado): the Inquisition, which the Grand Inquisitor transports to Seville.
images/art/berruguete-autodafe.jpg.alt: Saint Dominic on a platform presides over an auto-da-fé; below, the condemned at the stake

images/art/caravage-conversion-saint-pau.caption: Caravaggio, The Conversion of Saint Paul (1600-1601, Rome, Santa Maria del Popolo, Cerasi Chapel): Paul, the “Dysangelist” of Der Antichrist.
images/art/caravage-conversion-saint-pau.alt: Saul thrown from his horse, arms open towards the light

images/art/gerome-diogene.jpg.caption: Jean-Léon Gérôme, Diogenes (1860, Baltimore, Walters Art Museum): the lantern in broad daylight, model for the madman who seeks God in § 125 of The Gay Science.
images/art/gerome-diogene.jpg.alt: Diogenes sitting in his jar lights a lantern, surrounded by dogs

images/art/titien-sisyphe.jpg.caption: Titian, Sisyphus (1548-1549, Madrid, Prado): the figure whom Camus makes the hero of the absurd.
images/art/titien-sisyphe.jpg.alt: Sisyphus carrying an enormous rock on his shoulders

images/art/michel-ange-creation-adam.jpg.caption: Michelangelo, The Creation of Adam, Sistine Chapel ceiling (c. 1511): man created in the image of God (Gn 1, 27), which Habermas seeks to translate into the secular language of dignity.
images/art/michel-ange-creation-adam.jpg.alt: God stretches out his finger towards that of the reclining Adam

images/art/temple-humanite-paris.jpg.caption: Façade of the Temple of Humanity, 5 rue Payenne, Paris: the positivist religion had its places of worship.
images/art/temple-humanite-paris.jpg.alt: Façade of the Temple of Humanity, rue Payenne, with a bust and an inscription

images/art/temple-positiviste-porto-aleg.caption: The Positivist Temple of Porto Alegre (Brazil): the cult of Humanity took root in Brazil, whose flag bears the Comtean motto Ordem e Progresso.
images/art/temple-positiviste-porto-aleg.alt: Columned façade of the Positivist Temple of Porto Alegre

images/art/raphael-ecole-athenes.jpg.caption: Raphael, The School of Athens (1509-1511, Vatican, Stanza della Segnatura): in the centre, Plato pointing to the sky and Aristotle stretching his hand towards the earth; on the left, the turbaned figure traditionally identified as Averroes.
images/art/raphael-ecole-athenes.jpg.alt: Greek philosophers gathered beneath ancient vaults around Plato and Aristotle

images/auteurs/platon.jpg.caption: Plato, Roman copy of the portrait made by Silanion c. 370 BCE for the Academy (Rome, Musei Capitolini).

images/auteurs/aristote.jpg.caption: Aristotle, Roman marble copy of a bronze by Lysippus (c. 330 BCE); the alabaster mantle is modern (Rome, Museo Nazionale Romano, Palazzo Altemps).

images/auteurs/plotin.jpg.caption: Marble head found at Ostia (3rd century CE, Ostia, Museo Ostiense), one of four replicas of the same portrait; the identification with Plotinus is traditional and disputed.

images/auteurs/averroes.jpg.caption: Averroes, detail of the Triumph of Saint Thomas Aquinas by Andrea di Bonaiuto, Spanish Chapel, Santa Maria Novella, Florence (c. 1365-1367); no authentic portrait exists, the effigy is conventional.

images/auteurs/maimonide.jpg.caption: Maimonides, imaginary portrait published in Blasio Ugolini's Thesaurus antiquitatum sacrarum (1744), from which modern effigies derive; no authentic portrait exists.

images/oeuvres/maimonide-moreh-nevukhim-.caption: Moreh Nevukhim (Guide for the Perplexed) in the Hebrew translation, illuminated manuscript dated 1347-1348 (Copenhagen, Royal Library, Cod. Heb. 37): a master teaches before the vault of heaven.
images/oeuvres/maimonide-moreh-nevukhim-.alt: Illuminated page of a Hebrew manuscript: a master seated beneath a starry sky teaches a group of standing men

images/auteurs/montaigne.jpg.caption: Michel de Montaigne, anonymous portrait sometimes attributed to Daniel Dumonstier (Chantilly, Musée Condé).

images/oeuvres/montaigne-exemplaire-bord.caption: Engraved title page of the Essais (Paris, Abel L'Angelier, 1588), in the Bordeaux Copy, which Montaigne covered with corrections and additions until his death (Bordeaux, Bibliothèque municipale).
images/oeuvres/montaigne-exemplaire-bord.alt: Engraved frontispiece of the Essais, 1588 edition, with handwritten corrections in the central cartouche

images/auteurs/descartes.jpg.caption: René Descartes, after Frans Hals (Paris, Musée du Louvre).

images/oeuvres/descartes-meditationes-16.caption: Title page of the first edition of the Meditationes de prima philosophia (Paris, Michel Soly, 1641), “in qua Dei existentia et animae immortalitas demonstratur”.
images/oeuvres/descartes-meditationes-16.alt: Title page in Latin of the Meditationes de prima philosophia, Paris, 1641

images/auteurs/leibniz.jpg.caption: Leibniz, portrait by Christoph Bernhard Francke (c. 1695, Brunswick, Herzog Anton Ulrich-Museum).

images/oeuvres/leibniz-theodicee-1734.jp.caption: Title page of the Essais de théodicée sur la bonté de Dieu, la liberté de l'homme et l'origine du mal, in the new Amsterdam edition (1734); the first edition appeared in 1710.
images/oeuvres/leibniz-theodicee-1734.jp.alt: Title page of the Essais de théodicée, Amsterdam, 1734

images/auteurs/rousseau.jpg.caption: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, pastel by Maurice Quentin de La Tour, replica of the portrait exhibited at the Salon of 1753 (Saint-Quentin, Musée Antoine-Lécuyer).

images/oeuvres/rousseau-emile-1762.jpg.caption: Title page of the first edition of Émile, ou De l'éducation (1762), whose Book IV contains the Profession of Faith of the Savoyard Vicar; the book was condemned in Paris and in Geneva.
images/oeuvres/rousseau-emile-1762.jpg.alt: Title page of Émile, ou De l'éducation, 1762

images/auteurs/ricoeur.jpg.caption: Paul Ricoeur (right) with Maarten van Buuren at the Cerisy-la-Salle colloquium, August 1988.

images/auteurs/wittgenstein.jpg.caption: Ludwig Wittgenstein, photograph by Moritz Nähr (1930).

images/oeuvres/wittgenstein-tractatus-19.caption: Title page of the first English edition of the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (1922), published simultaneously in London by Kegan Paul and in New York by Harcourt, Brace, with an introduction by Bertrand Russell.
images/oeuvres/wittgenstein-tractatus-19.alt: Title page of the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, 1922

images/art/friedrich-moine-bord-de-mer.j.caption: Caspar David Friedrich, The Monk by the Sea (1808-1810, Berlin, Alte Nationalgalerie): the solitary man before immensity, a figure of wonder that there should be a world rather than nothing.
images/art/friedrich-moine-bord-de-mer.j.alt: A tiny silhouette of a monk on a shore, facing a dark sea beneath an immense sky

images/art/david-mort-de-socrate.jpg.caption: Jacques-Louis David, The Death of Socrates (1787, New York, Metropolitan Museum of Art): condemned in 399 BCE for impiety (ἀσέβεια, asebeia) and corrupting the young, Socrates drinks the hemlock; David places at the foot of the bed an aged Plato, whom the Phaedo (59b) says was absent that day.
images/art/david-mort-de-socrate.jpg.alt: Socrates, seated on his bed, reaches for the cup of hemlock, surrounded by grief-stricken disciples

images/art/rembrandt-moise-tables.jpg.caption: Rembrandt, Moses Breaking the Tablets of the Law (1659, Berlin, Gemäldegalerie): it is debated whether he is breaking them (Ex 32, 19) or presenting them to the people; Moses is the prophet to whom God shows only his back (Ex 33, 23), that is, according to the Guide for the Perplexed (I, 54), only his attributes of action.
images/art/rembrandt-moise-tables.jpg.alt: Moses raises the tablets of the Law above his head with both hands

images/art/poussin-veau-d-or.jpg.caption: Nicolas Poussin, The Adoration of the Golden Calf (c. 1633-1634, London, National Gallery): the god made by human hands (Ex 32), an ancient figure of what Feuerbach generalizes: in God, man worships what he has himself projected.
images/art/poussin-veau-d-or.jpg.alt: The Hebrews dance in a ring around the golden calf raised on an altar; in the distance, Moses comes down from Sinai

images/art/leonard-cene.jpg.caption: Leonardo da Vinci, The Last Supper (1495-1498, Milan, refectory of Santa Maria delle Grazie): the bread and the wine, which the last pages of Das Wesen des Christenthums restore to their natural and human meaning.
images/art/leonard-cene.jpg.alt: Christ at the centre of a long table, surrounded by the twelve agitated apostles

images/art/holbein-christ-mort.jpg.caption: Hans Holbein the Younger, The Body of the Dead Christ in the Tomb (1521-1522, Basel, Kunstmuseum): before a copy of this painting in Rogozhin's house, Prince Myshkin says, in The Idiot (1868-1869), that it could make one lose one's faith.
images/art/holbein-christ-mort.jpg.alt: The emaciated body of the dead Christ, lying in profile in a narrow niche

images/art/caravage-incredulite-thomas.j.caption: Caravaggio, The Incredulity of Saint Thomas (c. 1601-1602, Potsdam, Sanssouci, Picture Gallery): faith that demands proof (Jn 20, 24-29), set against Hume's question of testimony to miracles.
images/art/caravage-incredulite-thomas.j.alt: Thomas thrusts his finger into the wound in Christ's side, watched by two apostles leaning in

images/art/demachy-fete-etre-supreme.jpg.caption: Pierre-Antoine Demachy, The Festival of the Supreme Being at the Champ-de-Mars, 8 June 1794 (20 Prairial Year II) (Paris, Musée Carnavalet): the civic cult of Robespierre, a reader of the civil religion of The Social Contract (IV, 8).
images/art/demachy-fete-etre-supreme.jpg.alt: An artificial mountain topped by a tree and a column in the middle of the Champ-de-Mars, surrounded by a crowd

images/art/la-tour-madeleine-veilleuse.j.caption: Georges de La Tour, The Magdalen with the Smoking Flame, known as the Terff Magdalen (c. 1640-1645, Paris, Musée du Louvre): the skull, the books and the flame, a meditation on death that joins the ancient spiritual exercise in Hadot's sense.
images/art/la-tour-madeleine-veilleuse.j.alt: A woman seated in darkness, her hand resting on a skull, gazes at the flame of a lamp

images/art/delacroix-jacob-ange.jpg.caption: Eugène Delacroix, Jacob Wrestling with the Angel (1854-1861, Paris, church of Saint-Sulpice, Chapel of the Holy Angels): the night struggle of Gn 32, 25-33, an image of faith as a singular ordeal before God.
images/art/delacroix-jacob-ange.jpg.alt: Beneath tall trees, Jacob grapples with an angel who holds him back effortlessly

images/art/grunewald-crucifixion-issenhe.caption: Matthias Grünewald, the Crucifixion from the Isenheim Altarpiece (1512-1516, Colmar, Musée Unterlinden): Karl Barth kept a reproduction of this panel above his desk, and the outstretched index finger of John the Baptist served him as a figure of witness.
images/art/grunewald-crucifixion-issenhe.alt: The crucified Christ with his tortured body, between the Virgin supported by John, Mary Magdalene, and John the Baptist pointing to the cross

images/art/zurbaran-agnus-dei.jpg.caption: Francisco de Zurbarán, Agnus Dei (c. 1635-1640, Madrid, Prado): the bound lamb of the sacrificial victim (Jn 1, 29), in which Girard reads the Christian revelation of the innocence of the scapegoat victim.
images/art/zurbaran-agnus-dei.jpg.alt: A lamb with bound legs, lying on a table against a black background

images/art/caravage-sacrifice-isaac.jpg.caption: Caravaggio, The Sacrifice of Isaac (c. 1603, Florence, Uffizi Gallery): human sacrifice suspended and replaced by the ram (Gn 22), a key moment in Girard's reading of the Bible.
images/art/caravage-sacrifice-isaac.jpg.alt: An angel stops the hand of Abraham, who holds the screaming Isaac under the knife; a ram comes forward

images/art/holbein-ambassadeurs.jpg.caption: Hans Holbein the Younger, The Ambassadors (1533, London, National Gallery): in the foreground, an anamorphic skull, legible only from an angle, amid the emblems of knowledge and power: death kept out of sight, which Becker places at the centre of The Denial of Death (1973).
images/art/holbein-ambassadeurs.jpg.alt: Two men standing on either side of a shelf laden with instruments; on the floor, a distorted oblique shape

images/art/gauguin-d-ou-venons-nous.jpg.caption: Paul Gauguin, Where Do We Come From? What Are We? Where Are We Going? (1897-1898, Boston, Museum of Fine Arts): the three questions inscribed on the canvas are those that religion is expected to answer.
images/art/gauguin-d-ou-venons-nous.jpg.alt: A large frieze of Tahitian figures, from child to old man, around a blue idol

images/art/sarcophage-junius-bassus.jpg.caption: Sarcophagus of Junius Bassus (359 CE, Vatican City, Treasury of Saint Peter's): a prefect of Rome who died a neophyte, he was buried beneath the first great sculpted programme of scenes from the Old and New Testaments; in the centre of the upper register, Christ enthroned between Peter and Paul.
images/art/sarcophage-junius-bassus.jpg.alt: Marble sarcophagus carved in two registers of biblical scenes separated by small columns

images/art/pantocrator-deesis-sainte-sop.caption: Christ Pantocrator from the Deesis mosaic (13th century, Istanbul, Hagia Sophia): the Christ-Logos of Byzantine theology, a distant heir of the doctrine of the mediating Logos that Philo worked out in Alexandria.
images/art/pantocrator-deesis-sainte-sop.alt: Face of Christ in mosaic on a gold ground, his right hand raised in blessing

images/art/christ-helios-mausolee-julii..caption: Vault mosaic of the Mausoleum of the Julii (Mausoleum M) in the necropolis beneath Saint Peter's in the Vatican (3rd century CE): the Sun on his chariot, interpreted as Christ-Helios, at the time when the apologists were claiming for Christ the language of the philosophers and of the pagan cults.
images/art/christ-helios-mausolee-julii..alt: Vault mosaic: a charioteer with a radiant head against a background of vine scrolls

images/art/botticelli-saint-augustin.jpg.caption: Sandro Botticelli, Saint Augustine in His Study (1480, Florence, church of Ognissanti), a fresco painted as a companion piece to Ghirlandaio's Saint Jerome.
images/art/botticelli-saint-augustin.jpg.alt: Saint Augustine in bishop's robes, his hand on his heart, looks up from his desk

images/art/rembrandt-apotre-paul.jpg.caption: Rembrandt (and workshop?), The Apostle Paul (c. 1657, Washington, National Gallery of Art): the apostle meditating before his letters, the sword of his martyrdom in his hand.
images/art/rembrandt-apotre-paul.jpg.alt: A bearded old man seated at a table before sheets of paper, his hand on the hilt of a sword

images/art/piero-resurrection.jpg.caption: Piero della Francesca, The Resurrection (c. 1463-1465, Sansepolcro, Museo Civico): the Christ of Easter faith, whom historical research distinguishes from the Jesus of history.
images/art/piero-resurrection.jpg.alt: Christ standing, one foot on the edge of the tomb, holding a banner, above sleeping soldiers

images/art/bon-pasteur-crypte-lucine.jpg.caption: The Good Shepherd, painting in the Crypt of Lucina, Catacomb of Callixtus (Rome, 3rd century CE), plate from Joseph Wilpert, Die Malereien der Katakomben Roms (1903): the imagery of the Church that Celsus attacks and that Origen defends in Against Celsus (c. 248).
images/art/bon-pasteur-crypte-lucine.jpg.alt: Wall painting: a shepherd carrying a sheep on his shoulders, between two other sheep

images/auteurs/philon.jpg.caption: Philo of Alexandria, imaginary portrait published in André Thevet's Les Vrais Pourtraits et vies des hommes illustres (1584); no authentic portrait exists, the effigy is conventional.

images/auteurs/justin.jpg.caption: Justin Martyr, imaginary portrait published in André Thevet's Les Vrais Pourtraits et vies des hommes illustres (1584); no authentic portrait exists, the effigy is conventional.

images/auteurs/origene.jpg.caption: Origen, detail of an imaginary portrait published in André Thevet's Les Vrais Pourtraits et vies des hommes illustres (1584); no authentic portrait exists, the effigy is conventional.

images/auteurs/augustin.jpg.caption: Saint Augustine, by Philippe de Champaigne (c. 1645-1650, Los Angeles County Museum of Art); an imaginary portrait, no authentic portrait exists.

images/auteurs/tylor.png.caption: Edward Burnett Tylor, photograph by the Elliott & Fry studio, published in Folk-Lore, vol. 28 (1917).

images/auteurs/frazer.jpg.caption: James George Frazer, bronze bust by Antoine Bourdelle (1922, Montauban, Musée Ingres-Bourdelle).

images/auteurs/malinowski.jpg.caption: Bronisław Malinowski, professor of anthropology at the London School of Economics, c. 1930 (LSE Library).

images/auteurs/clifford.jpg.caption: William Kingdon Clifford, portrait published in The Popular Science Monthly (1879), the year of his death: the author of “The Ethics of Belief” (1877).

images/auteurs/aron.png.caption: Raymond Aron in 1956, photograph by Studio Harcourt: the author of “L'avenir des religions séculières” (1944) and of L'Opium des intellectuels (1955).

images/art/bruegel-tour-babel.jpg.caption: Pieter Bruegel the Elder, The Tower of Babel (1563, Vienna, Kunsthistorisches Museum): the human work that claims to reach heaven, a figure of what Voegelin calls the immanentization of the eschaton, salvation carried from heaven into history and entrusted to human hands.
images/art/bruegel-tour-babel.jpg.alt: A colossal spiral tower, unfinished, rises above a port city; in the foreground, a king visits the building site

images/oeuvres/maimonide-dux-1520.jpg.caption: Title page of the Dux seu director dubitantium aut perplexorum (Paris, Josse Bade, 1520), the medieval Latin translation of Maimonides' Guide for the Perplexed, revised by Agostino Giustiniani (Munich, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek): the book that Leo Strauss makes the model of esoteric writing, which speaks to the few under the veil of the common teaching.
images/oeuvres/maimonide-dux-1520.jpg.alt: Engraved title page in a Renaissance frame, with a printing press at the centre

images/art/saenredam-caverne-platon.jpg.caption: Jan Saenredam after Cornelis van Haarlem, Plato's Cave (engraving, 1604, Washington, National Gallery of Art): the prisoners of the cave (Republic, Book VII); Murdoch makes this myth the pattern of the moral life, a conversion of attention that turns away from the self towards the Good.
images/art/saenredam-caverne-platon.jpg.alt: Engraving: men chained in a cave watch shadows cast by a fire, while daylight opens at the back

images/oeuvres/coran-birmingham.jpg.caption: Leaf of the Birmingham Quran manuscript (Cadbury Research Library, Mingana Collection), in Hijazi script; the parchment has been radiocarbon dated to between 568 and 645: one of the oldest witnesses to the Quranic text, at the heart of the historical reading of the Quran that Mohammed Arkoun called for.
images/oeuvres/coran-birmingham.jpg.alt: Parchment leaf covered in early, slanting Arabic script, without systematic diacritical dots

images/art/bouddha-gandhara.jpg.caption: Standing Buddha, Gandhara art, Peshawar region (Pakistan), Kushan period, 2nd-3rd century CE, schist (Tokyo National Museum): the Buddha draped like a Hellenistic orator, an early encounter between India and Greece long before European philosophers discovered Buddhism.
images/art/bouddha-gandhara.jpg.alt: Schist statue of a standing Buddha, wearing a deeply folded cloak, in the manner of a Greek statue

images/art/partie-naissance-christianism.caption: The Virgin and Child and a prophet pointing to a star, Catacomb of Priscilla (Rome, 3rd century CE), plate from Joseph Wilpert, Die Malereien der Katakomben Roms (1903).
images/art/partie-naissance-christianism.alt: Wall painting: a seated woman holding a child, and a standing man pointing to a star

images/art/partie-pourquoi-croit-on.jpg.caption: Gustave Courbet, A Burial at Ornans (1849-1850, Paris, Musée d'Orsay).
images/art/partie-pourquoi-croit-on.jpg.alt: A procession of villagers in black around an open grave, under a low sky

images/art/partie-prologue.jpg.caption: Francisco de Goya, The Sleep of Reason Produces Monsters, Caprichos no. 43 (1797-1799).
images/art/partie-prologue.jpg.alt: A man asleep at his work table, beset by bats and owls

images/art/partie-deuxieme.jpg.caption: Joseph Wright of Derby, A Philosopher Lecturing on the Orrery (c. 1766, Derby Museum).
images/art/partie-deuxieme.jpg.alt: Faces lit by the central lamp of a mechanical orrery

images/art/partie-troisieme.jpg.caption: Caspar David Friedrich, Wanderer above the Sea of Fog (c. 1818, Hamburg, Kunsthalle).
images/art/partie-troisieme.jpg.alt: A man seen from behind on a rock contemplates a sea of clouds

images/art/partie-quatrieme.jpg.caption: Adolph Menzel, The Iron Rolling Mill (Modern Cyclopes) (1872-1875, Berlin, Alte Nationalgalerie).
images/art/partie-quatrieme.jpg.alt: Sweating workers handle a red-hot iron bar in front of the machines of a rolling mill

images/art/partie-cinquieme.jpg.caption: Ivan Kramskoy, Christ in the Desert (1872, Moscow, Tretyakov Gallery).
images/art/partie-cinquieme.jpg.alt: A man sitting alone on rocks, hands clasped, in the light of dawn

images/art/partie-sixieme.jpg.caption: Jules Breton, The Blessing of the Wheat in Artois (1857): lived religion, the object of the sciences of religion.
images/art/partie-sixieme.jpg.alt: A village procession with canopy and banners crossing a wheat field

images/art/partie-septieme.jpg.caption: Caspar David Friedrich, The Abbey in the Oakwood (1809-1810, Berlin, Alte Nationalgalerie).
images/art/partie-septieme.jpg.alt: A ruined Gothic abbey surrounded by bare oaks in the mist

images/art/partie-huitieme.jpg.caption: Notre-Dame de Paris, c. 1890-1900 (Library of Congress).
images/art/partie-huitieme.jpg.alt: Façade of Notre-Dame de Paris in photochrom

images/art/partie-neuvieme.jpg.caption: Equestrian statue of Marcus Aurelius on the Piazza del Campidoglio in Rome (replica; the bronze original is in the Capitoline Museums).
images/art/partie-neuvieme.jpg.alt: Bronze equestrian statue of Marcus Aurelius, his arm outstretched

images/art/partie-conclusion.jpg.caption: Caspar David Friedrich, Woman before the Setting Sun (c. 1818, Essen, Museum Folkwang).
images/art/partie-conclusion.jpg.alt: A woman seen from behind, arms open, facing the low sun

images/art/partie-anciens-monotheismes.j.caption: Plato's Academy, mosaic from the villa of T. Siminius Stephanus in Pompeii (1st century BCE, Naples, Museo Archeologico Nazionale).
images/art/partie-anciens-monotheismes.j.alt: Seven philosophers seated in a semicircle beneath a tree, before the walls of a city

images/art/partie-age-classique.jpg.caption: Johannes Vermeer, The Astronomer (1668, Paris, Musée du Louvre).
images/art/partie-age-classique.jpg.alt: A scholar in a robe reaches towards a celestial globe set near a window
